article_title: Supporting interdisciplinary collaborative concept mapping with individual preparation phase
citation: Esther Tan, Jacob Gerolf de Weerd, Slavi Stoyanov. (2021). Supporting interdisciplinary collaborative concept mapping with individual preparation phase. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09963-w
title: Epistemic and social process framework for collaborative knowledge co-construction and transactivity
description: The article organises collaborative knowledge co-construction along two dimensions. The epistemic dimension uses Beers et al.'s (2006) 'primitives of negotiation' — contribution, clarification, verification, elaboration — plus the authors' added positioning. The social dimension uses Weinberger and Fischer's (2006) five social modes: "externalisation, elicitation, quick-consensus building, integration-oriented consensus building and conflict-oriented consensus building", which represent different levels of transactivity, with conflict-oriented consensus building the highest. The study applies this framework as coding schemes to audio-recorded collaborative discourse.
requirements: Discourse data coded by trained independent raters with sufficient inter-rater reliability (Cohen's Kappa κ = 0.79 epistemic, κ = 0.88 social)
constraints: Transactivity levels are inferred from nominal-level coded discourse categories rather than direct measures
target_learners: third-year university students in interdisciplinary minors
target_learning_goals: interdisciplinary knowledge integration
collaborative knowledge co-construction
examples: Audio recordings of eight groups' collaborative concept mapping were coded into the epistemic categories and the five social modes, then compared across WIP and WOIP with chi-square tests.
key_sources: Esther Tan, Jacob Gerolf de Weerd, Slavi Stoyanov. (2021). Supporting interdisciplinary collaborative concept mapping with individual preparation phase. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09963-w

article_title: Refining qualitative ethnographies using Epistemic Network Analysis: A study of socioemotional learning dimensions in a Humanistic Knowledge Building Community
citation: Hod, Yotam; Eagan, Brendan; Katz, Shir. (2020). Refining qualitative ethnographies using Epistemic Network Analysis: A study of socioemotional learning dimensions in a humanistic knowledge building community. Journal article. https://zenodo.org
title: Epistemic Network Analysis as a methodology for producing quantitative ethnographies of complex learning environments
description: Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) is described as "a methodology for producing quantitative ethnographies based on complex learning environments." The study uses ENA to analyze data collected during a semester of studies in a classroom learning community, applying it to socioemotional facets of learning, which the article notes ENA "has only begun to examine." ENA is positioned as complementary to deep, qualitative ethnography rather than a replacement for it.
requirements: Data collected from a complex learning environment over time, as in the semester of studies analyzed here
constraints: The article states ENA has only begun to examine socioemotional facets of learning in classrooms
target_learning_goals: socioemotional dimensions of learning
sociocognitive development in knowledge building communities
examples: The authors employed ENA to analyze a semester of data from a humanistic knowledge building community, in parallel with a stage developmental qualitative analysis.

article_title: Factors influencing the incorporation of Entrustable Professional Activities into assessment in nutrition and dietetics education: A systematic review.
citation: Surace R, Palermo C, Porter J. (2025). Factors influencing the incorporation of Entrustable Professional Activities into assessment in nutrition and dietetics education: A systematic review. Nutrition & Dietetics. https://doi.org/10.1111/1747-0080.70004
title: EPAs as a tool to support shared understanding and simplicity of judgments in competency-based assessment.
description: The review frames EPAs not as the definitive solution to the complexity of competency-based assessment but rather as a tool to support a shared understanding and simplicity of judgments. EPAs show promise in supporting the untangling of complex CBA by offering a practical, clearly visible, and easily understood authentic form of assessment for assessors and learners, which is outcomes-based and complements existing competency frameworks.
requirements: Linkage to existing competency frameworks.
constraints: EPAs should not be considered the definitive solution to the complexity of competency-based assessment.
target_learning_goals: work-readiness assessment

article_title: Interventions to improve pharmacists' competency in chronic disease management: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials.
citation: Rendrayani Farida, Utami Auliasari M., Insani Widya N., Puspita Falerina, Alfian Sofa D., Nguyen Thang, Puspitasari Irma M. (2024). Interventions to improve pharmacists’ competency in chronic disease management: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06393-z
title: EPOC taxonomy of intervention types for classifying health-professional competency interventions
description: The Cochrane Effective Practice and Organization of Care (EPOC) taxonomy classifies health-system interventions into four types. The review states: "Using the latest EPOC taxonomy [37], the interventions were further categorized into four types" — delivery arrangements, financial arrangements, governance arrangements, and implementation strategies — and uses it to organize its synthesis, arguing the taxonomy "ensures consistent classification and comparability" for decision-makers. In the included studies only implementation strategies and combined implementation strategies–delivery arrangements types appeared.
requirements: Interventions must be classifiable into one of the four EPOC types for consistent classification and comparability
constraints: No financial arrangements or governance arrangements interventions appeared among the 11 included RCTs
target_learners: pharmacists in community and hospital settings
target_learning_goals: knowledge, skills, and attitudes for chronic disease management
examples: The review classified all 11 included RCTs as implementation strategies (n = 8) or combined implementation strategies–delivery arrangements (n = 3)

article_title: Using an e-Portfolio System to Improve the Academic Writing Performance of ESL Students
citation: Ali Alshahrani and Scott Windeatt. (2012). Using an e-Portfolio System to Improve the Academic Writing Performance of ESL Students. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://research-publishing.net
title: E-portfolio-supported process writing with peer and teacher feedback
description: The pattern uses a web-based e-portfolio system (TaskStream) as a framework within which ESL students work through the key phases of the writing process — pre-writing, drafting and revising — while writing for an audience of peers. The system "allowed learners to write for an audience (each other) and to give feedback to, and receive feedback from, both their intended audience, and their teacher". It aims to develop self-consistency, positive writing self-belief, and realistic self-judgement of strengths and weaknesses as writers.
requirements: Appropriate, regular feedback from peers and the teacher while learners work through planning, drafting and revising stages
A web-based e-portfolio system through which essays are submitted and feedback exchanged
constraints: The article notes e-portfolio use will probably increase the length of time required to cover the curriculum
target_learners: ESL students on intensive English language writing courses
target_learning_goals: Academic writing performance
Writing self-efficacy and self-belief
Consistent application of the writing process approach
examples: 46 ESL students from an English language centre were divided into a conventional group and an experimental e-portfolio group and submitted a series of essays over a number of weeks, receiving peer and teacher feedback
key_sources: Ali Alshahrani and Scott Windeatt. (2012). Using an e-Portfolio System to Improve the Academic Writing Performance of ESL Students. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED574901

article_title: Using an e-Portfolio System to Improve the Academic Writing Performance of ESL Students
citation: Ali Alshahrani and Scott Windeatt. (2012). Using an e-Portfolio System to Improve the Academic Writing Performance of ESL Students. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://research-publishing.net
title: Use e-portfolios to give learners control of goal-setting, identity presentation and progress monitoring in writing courses
description: The article argues e-portfolios benefit learners by letting them "control their learning by setting their own learning goals and the time line within which these goals are to be achieved", by supporting identity presentation and interaction with teachers, peers and external reviewers, and by recording academic development so as to promote metacognitive skills including monitoring and evaluation of progress. Learners can also share, collaborate and scaffold each other while learning.
requirements: An e-portfolio system that records learners' academic development and supports interaction with teachers, peers and external reviewers
target_learning_goals: Self-directed learning
Metacognitive monitoring and evaluation of progress
Collaborative meaning construction
examples: In the study, e-portfolio students wrote for each other and received feedback from peers and the teacher across a series of essays

article_title: E-Portfolio as a Corrective Platform towards EFL Students' Overall/Componential Writing Performance
citation: Saeedi, Z., & Meihami, H. (2015). E-Portfolio as a Corrective Platform towards EFL Students' Overall/Componential Writing Performance. Teaching English with Technology, 15(4), 76-97. http://www.tewtjournal.org
title: E-portfolio as a corrective feedback platform grounded in cognitive learning theory and self-regulation
description: The article frames EP-based corrective feedback within cognitive learning theory supporting deep learning processes of "creating, implementing, and evaluating L2". It explains the observed writing gains through self-regulation: feedback received via EP contributes to "feedback internalization" because students feel more responsible for their learning. EP's asynchronous, face-saving nature also lowers the affective filter, reducing anxiety compared with public corrective feedback.
requirements: Students must understand the corrective feedback platform to utilize the feedback received
constraints: Effectiveness depends on students' awareness of EP; without awareness, students may ignore implicit feedback
target_learning_goals: L2 writing improvement through internalized corrective feedback

article_title: Feasibility and implementation of a final year Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) in a medical model curriculum.
citation: Noll C, Mikuteit M, Golon S, Louzek C, Afshar K, Just I, Steffens S. (2026). Feasibility and implementation of a final year Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) in a medical model curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10350-3
title: A structured, EPA-based station development process with interdisciplinary workshops and modified Angoff standard-setting.
description: The article describes a reproducible pattern for developing OSCE stations: an interdisciplinary team develops stations based on Entrustable Professional Activities, refines them in structured workshops involving students and standardised patient programme representatives, and sets pass–fail cut scores using the modified Angoff method. Stations were designed so that "at least 50.0% of the stations had to include a practical clinical skill", and each station included at least one communication subtask. This pattern enabled rapid design of 34 stations by subject-matter experts.
requirements: Requires an interdisciplinary project team with medical education, examination design, and specialist clinical knowledge.
Requires structured workshops with station developers, students, PJ-OSCE team members, and a standardised patient programme representative.
constraints: The article notes this was implemented within the specific curricular context of the HannibaL model curriculum at Hannover Medical School and the German medical licensing framework.
target_learners: Final-year undergraduate medical students prior to the Practical Year
target_learning_goals: Practical clinical skills
Clinical decision-making
Physician–patient communication
Interprofessional communication
examples: 34 PJ-OSCE stations were developed by 17 specialist physicians and five students, with 82.3% including clinical decision-making elements and 76.5% containing a skill.

Clinical competencies

article_title: Identifying clinical skill gaps of healthcare workers using a digital clinical decision support algorithm during outpatient pediatric consultations in primary health centers in Rwanda.
citation: Karoui Haykel, Rwandarwacu Victor P., Niyonzima Jonathan, Makuza Antoinette, Nkuranga John B., D'Acremont Valérie, Kulinkina Alexandra V. (2025). Identifying clinical skill gaps of healthcare workers using a digital clinical decision support algorithm during outpatient pediatric consultations in primary health centers in Rwanda. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318284
title: ePOCT+ digital IMCI-based clinical decision support algorithm for outpatient pediatric care
description: ePOCT+ (electronic point of care tests plus) is a tablet-based digital clinical decision support algorithm implemented in 16 primary health centers in Rwanda as part of the DYNAMIC project. The article describes it as "a digital IMCI-based CDSA created to improve the quality of outpatient care for children under 15 years of age". Healthcare workers input anthropometric measures, vital signs, and symptom/sign presence following a logical consultation flow; the algorithm proposes diagnostic tests, then clinical diagnoses with management guidelines that can be accepted or rejected. All inputs are mandatory, with a limited 'not feasible' option, and it includes point-of-care devices such as pulse oximetry, hemoglobin and C-reactive protein measurement.
requirements: Accurate inputs (symptoms and signs) entered by healthcare workers, which relies on their clinical skills
Real-time use: perform the assessment, input the result, then move to the next proposed task
constraints: The article notes the dataset may be biased toward negative responses when healthcare workers answer without conducting the assessment
Alerts were unavailable to triage staff who wrote values on paper for later entry, and some inadequate measurements did not trigger alert thresholds
target_learners: healthcare workers in primary health centers in Rwanda
target_learning_goals: guiding outpatient pediatric consultations and proposing diagnoses and management plans
examples: Used for 20,085 consultations between November 2021 and October 2022 whose log data formed the retrospective analysis
key_sources: Karoui Haykel, Rwandarwacu Victor P., Niyonzima Jonathan, Makuza Antoinette, Nkuranga John B., D'Acremont Valérie, Kulinkina Alexandra V. (2025). Identifying clinical skill gaps of healthcare workers using a digital clinical decision support algorithm during outpatient pediatric consultations in primary health centers in Rwanda. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318284

article_title: Evaluation of an e-learning platform promoting electronic personal health record competence: a pilot trial in older adults.
citation: Perotti Luis, Stamm Oskar, Ferizaj Drin, Dietrich Michael, Buchem Ilona, Müller-Werdan Ursula. (2025). Evaluation of an e-learning platform promoting electronic personal health record competence: a pilot trial in older adults. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-22242-0
title: ePA Coach: a microlearning-based e-learning platform with interactive ePHR mockups and a chat-based learning assistant for older adults
description: ePA Coach is a high-fidelity prototype learning platform developed as an "empowerment tool for self-sufficient ePHR usage". It offers 32 multimedia learning units (video and text, six to eight minutes each) across five competencies (basics, managing, adding, sharing and securing health data), organized into beginner, advanced and expert levels based on the EU DigComp framework, with gamification elements designed via the Octalysis framework. Interactive ePHR mockups let users practice navigation and tasks without real health data, and an always-available chat-based assistant built on RASA Conversational AI (107 intents, 1439 example questions, 217 responses) answers platform and ePHR questions; a moderated peer forum and glossary supplement the units.
requirements: Internet access and a device to access websites; participants needed basic digital skills to use the platform as a website
constraints: The article states that due to the design of the ePA Coach as a website, only those with access to the internet and basic digital skills could be included in the study
target_learners: Young-old adults aged 50–64 and older adults aged 65+ in Germany learning to use the electronic patient file (ePA)
target_learning_goals: ePHR knowledge, ePHR operation skills, and attitudes toward using the ePHR
examples: In the pilot trial, both age groups completed almost 80% of the 32 learning units during the one-week intervention period
key_sources: Perotti Luis, Stamm Oskar, Ferizaj Drin, Dietrich Michael, Buchem Ilona, Müller-Werdan Ursula. (2025). Evaluation of an e-learning platform promoting electronic personal health record competence: a pilot trial in older adults. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-22242-0

article_title: How Do Trainees Use EPAs to Regulate Their Learning in the Clinical Environment? A Grounded Theory Study.
citation: Thoonen Bart P. A., Scherpbier-de Haan Nynke D., Fluit Cornelia R. M. G., Stalmeijer Renée E. (2024). How Do Trainees Use EPAs to Regulate Their Learning in the Clinical Environment? A Grounded Theory Study. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.1403
title: Three-stage model of trainees' EPA use across placements: adaptation, taking control, and checking the boxes
description: The article constructs a grounded theory in which trainees self-regulate learning by balancing helping and hindering influences of EPAs across three consecutive stages. As printed: "Three consecutive stages were constructed each with different use of EPAs: adaptation, taking control, and checking the boxes." Each stage appeared in both first and final year placements, with the adaptation phase typically shorter in the final year. The model was built from ten interviews plus two PICTOR interviews using constant comparative analysis.
requirements: Placements must be long enough for trainees to move from adaptation into the taking-control stage
constraints: Constructed from a single GP-training case at one Dutch medical centre; the authors note theoretical sufficiency may not have been fully achieved
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning in the clinical workplace
examples: Trainees in the adaptation phase deferred EPA use, while in the taking-control stage they scheduled specific patients and set learning objectives using EPAs

article_title: Skill retention following simulation learning in acute coronary syndrome versus cardiac arrest.
citation: Ghazali Hanen, Ouaness Islem, Zaouch Khedija, Hamed Rym, Ines Chermiti, Manai Hela. (2022). Skill retention following simulation learning in acute coronary syndrome versus cardiac arrest. La Tunisie Médicale. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9703463/
title: Episodic memory as the proposed mechanism for simulation-based learning and its retention
description: The article proposes episodic memory as one explanation of how simulator training produces learning and retention. It defines it as "la capacité d'un individu à se souvenir d'un événement vécu (sur simulateur) et de sa faculté à ressortir consciemment les informations mémorisées lorsqu'il revivra un événement identique (dans le réel)", i.e. recalling a lived simulated event and consciously retrieving the stored information when an identical event recurs in real practice. The article presents this as an advanced explanation rather than a mechanism tested in the study.
requirements: Exposure to a lived simulated event that can later be consciously recalled when an identical real event occurs
constraints: The article offers this as an explanatory concept cited from prior work, not as a mechanism tested in its own data
target_learners: young family-medicine residents in emergency departments
target_learning_goals: management of cardiac arrest and acute coronary syndrome emergencies
examples: The authors invoke episodic memory when discussing why simulator training may produce durable skills, citing prior work on difficult-airway mannequin training

article_title: Using an Entrustable Professional Activity to Assess Consultation Requests Called on an Internal Medicine Teaching Service.
citation: Kang Angela J., Gielissen Katherine, Windish Donna. (2019). Using an Entrustable Professional Activity to Assess Consultation Requests Called on an Internal Medicine Teaching Service. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10854
title: EPA-based consultation-request assessment instrument set (EPA document, Resident Supervisor Instrument, Intern Self-Reflection Instrument)
description: A set of three instruments built from an EPA delineating the knowledge, skills, and attitudes required to call a consultation request, developed from ACGME milestones, ten Cate et al.'s framework, Goldman's principles, and the PICO framework. The resident instrument assesses "the critical actions observable while the consultation request was being called," and the intern instrument supports self-reflection after feedback. Appendices A–E provide the EPA document, both instruments, an item-to-EPA correlation guide, and usage guidelines.
requirements: Participants received approximately 10 minutes of training on the use of the assessment instruments on the first or second day of their inpatient rotation
constraints: Not all critical actions from the EPA are assessed by items on the Resident Supervisor Instrument
The final critical action, "Intern follows up on consultation recommendations," was not observable during the call and was not evaluated
target_learning_goals: calling consultation requests
formulating PICO-centered clinical questions
calibrating required supervision level
examples: Used on two internal medicine inpatient teaching services at Yale New Haven Hospital from April through June of 2018, yielding 26 paired observations

article_title: Predicting Bullying through Motivation and Teaching Styles in Physical Education.
citation: Montero-Carretero C., Barbado D., Cervelló E. (2020). Predicting Bullying through Motivation and Teaching Styles in Physical Education. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17010087
title: Questionnaire battery measuring supportive style, need satisfaction, motivation, and bullying in PE
description: The study used four validated self-report instruments: the EPES-PE (19 items measuring organizational, procedural, and cognitive autonomy support plus controlling style, α = 0.94 for global AS), the Basic Psychological Needs in Exercise Scale adapted to PE (12 items, global α = 0.90), the CMPE motivation questionnaire (20 items across five motivation factors), and the Spanish European Bullying Intervention Project Questionnaire (EBIP-Q, 14 items, α = 0.83 for both perpetration and victimization).
requirements: Completed by students in approximately 20 minutes during a scheduled PE class with teacher clarification of doubts
constraints: Exclusive use of self-reports, noted by the authors as a main limitation
target_learning_goals: Assessment of teaching style, motivation, need satisfaction, and bullying behaviors in PE
key_sources: Montero-Carretero C., Barbado D., Cervelló E. (2020). Predicting Bullying through Motivation and Teaching Styles in Physical Education. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17010087

article_title: Feasibility of the Epiduroscopy Simulator as a Training Tool: A Pilot Study.
citation: Lee Jong Joo, Ko Junho, Yun Yeomin, Jang Seong-Wook, Ha Yoon, Kim Yoon Sang, Shin Dong Ah. (2020). Feasibility of the Epiduroscopy Simulator as a Training Tool: A Pilot Study. Pain Research & Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/2020/5428170
title: EpiduroSIM: a virtual epiduroscopy simulator with joystick control and dual epiduroscopic/fluoroscopic views
description: EpiduroSIM is a virtual simulator built from a DICOM set of human CT data converted to 3D geometry and rendered in Unity 3D, controlled with a joystick. It "consists of three parts: visualization, training, and evaluation", models the spinal canal, intervertebral discs, dural sac, and spinal nerves, and displays both epiduroscopic and fluoroscopic views. It scores performance from an initial 100 points, deducting points for collisions and time, and records time to target, total score, and number of violations.
requirements: Requires additional equipment to operate, including a laptop and joystick controller
constraints: It is not available for commercial purchase
A haptic device was developed but not used because of a technical limitation in the actual experiments
target_learning_goals: catheter navigation to a target lesion site in the epidural space
anatomical understanding of the catheter insertion pathway
avoiding dura and nerve violation during epiduroscopy
examples: 20 physicians each performed the simulator 20 times in one day, navigating the catheter tip from the sacral hiatus to the posterior part of the L4-5 intervertebral disc without touching nerve or dura

article_title: Facilitating learning of community-based rehabilitation through problem-based learning in higher education.
citation: Chung Eva Yin-han. (2019). Facilitating learning of community-based rehabilitation through problem-based learning in higher education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1868-4
title: E-portfolios as documentation and assessment tools for PBL processes and outcomes
description: In this study, each group submitted an e-portfolio at the end of the course showing the outcomes of learning and allowing the instructor to assess how well students had acquired and applied knowledge. E-portfolios are personalised, web-based collections of work and reflections, managed online so students can maintain them dynamically over time. The article states they are "particularly suitable for PBL because they enable students to organise and reflect on knowledge acquired in classes". Students used various platforms, including some enabling social communication among members, though mastering IT skills was a common obstacle.
requirements: A good infrastructure providing sufficient technical support to students, including library resources, hardware, and IT support
constraints: Students encountered technical difficulties and found learning the compilation software difficult
target_learners: Undergraduate health science students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: Organising, documenting, and reflecting on learning processes and outcomes
examples: Groups produced microfilms, video clips, and animations, with diagrammatic presentation such as flow charts and mind maps

article_title: Ward round competences in surgery and psychiatry - a comparative multidisciplinary interview study.
citation: Vietz E, März E, Lottspeich C, Wölfel T, Fischer MR, Schmidmaier R. (2019). Ward round competences in surgery and psychiatry - a comparative multidisciplinary interview study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1554-6
title: Entrustable professional activity (EPA) framework for teaching and assessing ward round practice
description: The entrustable professional activity (EPA) concept, devised by Ten Cate in 2005, links all competences needed for a clinical task to that task so it can be entrusted to a trainee once sufficient competence is reached. The article defines EPAs as "tasks or responsibilities that can be entrusted to a trainee once sufficient, specific competence is reached to allow for unsupervised execution". It proposes an EPA "Conducting a ward round" built on the identified competence list, usable with competency frameworks such as ACGME or CanMEDS, and notes the existing EPA for internal medicine ward rounds can serve as a basis for other specialities.
requirements: The general competences would have to be further divided into more specific subcompetences and linked to their observable tasks before an EPA can be developed
constraints: The identified competences represent the status quo of ward round practice in Germany and have to be proven for general validity
target_learning_goals: conducting a ward round
ward round competences
examples: A related prior study proposed an EPA "Conducting an internal medicine ward round" with overlapping competences, which the authors suggest transferring to surgery and psychiatry bearing in mind the differences

article_title: Using electronic patient records: defining learning outcomes for undergraduate education.
citation: Pontefract S. K., Wilson K. (2019). Using electronic patient records: defining learning outcomes for undergraduate education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1466-5
title: Teach EPR competencies undergraduates because students are rarely exposed to the technology during training
description: The article argues healthcare students need structured opportunities to develop EPR competencies during undergraduate training because exposure is currently lacking: "Healthcare students are rarely exposed to the technology, or given the opportunity to use this during their training, which can impact on the digital competence of the graduating workforce." Training is described as essential for successful implementation and ongoing use of the technology, and lack of training, education and staff development have been identified as major barriers to innovation. Existing workforce digital-readiness initiatives do not include the future workforce—healthcare students.
requirements: Training should occur within an environment made safe for learning, with opportunities to develop competencies to access, discriminate, analyse, apply knowledge and master large flows of information
constraints: Sub-optimal use of EPRs can increase the risk of clinical and procedural errors
target_learners: undergraduate healthcare students in medicine, pharmacy, nursing and midwifery
target_learning_goals: digital competence for working in a digital healthcare environment
safe and effective delivery of care with EPRs
examples: NHS England committed to making all patient care records digital, real-time and interoperable by 2023, increasing student exposure to EPR systems
key_sources: Pontefract S. K., Wilson K. (2019). Using electronic patient records: defining learning outcomes for undergraduate education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1466-5

article_title: Changing Autonomy in Operative Experience Through UK General Surgery Training: A National Cohort Study.
citation: Elsey EJ, Griffiths G, West J, Humes DJ. (2018). Changing Autonomy in Operative Experience Through UK General Surgery Training: A National Cohort Study. Annals of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/SLA.0000000000003032
title: Entrustable Professional Activity supervision levels as a lens for interpreting logbook autonomy as evidence of entrustment
description: The article applies the entrustable professional activity framework, in which an EPA is "a unit of activity undertaken which the trainee could be trusted to complete," to surgical training. It maps ten Cate's five supervision levels onto the UK eLogbook supervision codes (Assisting; Supervised, Trainer Scrubbed; Supervised, Trainer Unscrubbed; Performed; Training a more junior trainee) and distinguishes ad hoc from summative entrustment decisions. On this account, a trainee routinely recorded as performing a procedure unsupervised has plausibly been entrusted with it, so longitudinal logbook supervision patterns across a whole cohort can evidence changing entrustment decisions alongside formal competency assessments.
requirements: Requires routinely collected operative records coding each procedure by supervision level, and formal competency assessments (PBAs) to triangulate the autonomy evidence
constraints: The article states supervised versus unsupervised operating "does not necessarily reflect a trainee's capability to perform a procedure but may merely reflect who was present in theater," limiting entrustment conclusions from logbook data alone
target_learning_goals: Operative procedural competency and readiness for independent practice
examples: The study mapped supervision codes for 311 trainees across an entire 6-year program and linked the rising unsupervised proportions to level 4 PBA award patterns
key_sources: Elsey EJ, Griffiths G, West J, Humes DJ. (2018). Changing Autonomy in Operative Experience Through UK General Surgery Training: A National Cohort Study. Annals of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1097/SLA.0000000000003032

article_title: Proficiency-based progression training: an 'end to end' model for decreasing error applied to achievement of effective epidural analgesia during labour: a randomised control study.
citation: Kallidaikurichi Srinivasan Karthikeyan, Gallagher Anthony, O'Brien Niall, Sudir Vinod, Barrett Nick, O'Connor Raymund, Holt Francesca, Lee Peter, O'Donnell Brian, Shorten George. (2018). Proficiency-based progression training: an 'end to end' model for decreasing error applied to achievement of effective epidural analgesia during labour: a randomised control study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2017-020099
title: Metrics-based epidural catheter placement assessment tool (74 procedure-specific metrics)
description: An assessment instrument consisting of 74 procedure-specific metrics for labour epidural catheter placement, each representing either an error or a critical error, with dichotomous yes-or-no scoring of observable behaviour. It was developed from expert input across five face-to-face meetings, stress-tested against reference videos, and validated by two blinded independent assessors. The article reports it achieved an inter-rater reliability of 0.88 and differentiated trainees from experts, unlike Likert-scale checklists and global rating scales.
requirements: Metrics must be observable on reference videos and defined objectively and explicitly
Assessors must be trained until inter-rater reliability of 0.8 or above is achieved
constraints: For this procedure all metrics were defined in terms of errors, and validation required videos showing all possible errors, which limited eligible video material
target_learners: Novice anaesthetic trainees learning labour epidural catheter placement
target_learning_goals: Objective assessment of procedural performance and provision of specific error-based feedback
examples: Two assessors blinded to operator category scored anonymised first-person videos recorded with wearable camera-mounted glasses

article_title: Faculty Beliefs about Intelligence Are Related to the Adoption of Active-Learning Practices.
citation: Aragón, O. R., Eddy, S. L., & Graham, M. J. (2018). Faculty Beliefs about Intelligence Are Related to the Adoption of Active-Learning Practices. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 17(3). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-05-0084
title: EPIC-implementation model of instructional-practice adoption
description: The EPIC-implementation model conceptualizes instructors' adoption of new teaching strategies as a multistage process. As the article states, "The model of adoption developed by Aragón and Graham (2015) recognizes five stages: exposure, persuasion, identification, commitment, and implementation (EPIC-implementation)." It was designed as an open framework inclusive of motivation, goal, and change theories, in which additional factors affecting adoption can be tested, and it serves as a diagnostic for identifying where along the adoption pathway an intervention might be modified.
requirements: Educators must first be clearly exposed to the proposed teaching method, with basic memory for and understanding of the proposed change, before later stages can be assessed.
constraints: The article states that meeting the thresholds of exposure, persuasion, and identification before commitment does not indicate a causal process; persuasion and identification are measured independently because thinking an activity is good and thinking it is good for one's self are dissociable constructs.
target_learning_goals: Adoption and sustained implementation of evidence-based active-learning teaching practices
examples: The survey asked respondents to endorse, for each of seven active-learning practices, whether they were exposed, convinced, found it compatible, decided to incorporate it, and implemented it.
key_sources: Aragón, O. R., Eddy, S. L., & Graham, M. J. (2018). Faculty Beliefs about Intelligence Are Related to the Adoption of Active-Learning Practices. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 17(3). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-05-0084

article_title: Knowledge, competencies and attitudes regarding external post-mortem physical examination: A survey among German post-graduate trainees in general practice.
citation: Valentini Jan, Goetz Katja, Yen Kathrin, Szecsenyi Joachim, Dettling Andrea, Joos Stefanie, Steinhaeuser Jost, Flum Elisabeth. (2018). Knowledge, competencies and attitudes regarding external post-mortem physical examination: A survey among German post-graduate trainees in general practice. The European Journal of General Practice. https://doi.org/10.1080/13814788.2017.1389884
title: 19-item questionnaire on knowledge, competencies and attitudes regarding the external post-mortem examination
description: A self-report questionnaire developed from a literature review and the work experiences of two GP authors, consisting of "19 items related to three main categories: knowledge, competencies and attitudes." Items use three-point scales (adequate/half-and-half/inadequate; yes/no; positive/neutral/negative) covering general and procedural knowledge, confidence in specific EPME tasks such as determining cause and time of death, and attitudes toward the examination. It was distributed by the lecturer before EPME courses and completed anonymously.
requirements: Anonymous, voluntary completion distributed by the lecturer before an EPME training course
constraints: The article states the narrow three-point Likert scale was susceptible to poorly differentiated data
target_learning_goals: Self-assessment of EPME knowledge, competencies and attitudes
examples: Administered to 380 trainees attending educational meetings, with 128 completed questionnaires returned (response rate 33.7%)

article_title: Trust, Growth Mindset, and Student Commitment to Active Learning in a College Science Course.
citation: Cavanagh A. J., Chen X., Bathgate M., Frederick J., Hanauer D. I., Graham M. J. (2018). Trust, Growth Mindset, and Student Commitment to Active Learning in a College Science Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-06-0107
title: EPIC framework: exposure–persuasion–identification–commitment model of student buy-in to active learning
description: The EPIC framework describes a staged buy-in process through which students move from being exposed to active learning, to being persuaded of its value, to identifying with it personally, to committing to engage in such practices in the future. As the article states, "The exposure–persuasion–identification–commitment (EPIC) framework aims to describe inevitable variations in the level of student commitment to active learning within a course." In this study, student commitment was operationalized as self-reported responses to 16 active-learning practices scored across the four EPIC subscales, and the framework structures the predictor–outcome analyses of trust and growth mindset.
requirements: Students must be exposed to active-learning practices and self-report their persuasion, identification, and commitment responses to those practices.
constraints: The framework was applied within a single course with one instructor; the article calls its findings exploratory and preliminary.
target_learners: undergraduate science majors in large active-learning courses
target_learning_goals: commitment to and engagement in active-learning practices
examples: Students rated 16 active-learning practices on dichotomous items across exposure, persuasion, identification, and commitment subscales, with KR20 reliabilities from 0.87 to 0.93.
key_sources: Cavanagh A. J., Chen X., Bathgate M., Frederick J., Hanauer D. I., Graham M. J. (2018). Trust, Growth Mindset, and Student Commitment to Active Learning in a College Science Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-06-0107

article_title: Student Buy-In to Active Learning in a College Science Course.
citation: Cavanagh A. J., Aragón O. R., Chen X., Couch B., Durham M., Bobrownicki A., Hanauer D. I., Graham M. J. (2016). Student Buy-In to Active Learning in a College Science Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education 15(4). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-07-0212
title: The EPIC process model of student buy-in to active learning
description: The exposure–persuasion–identification–commitment (EPIC) model is a four-stage process account of how students come to embrace active learning. As the authors state, "This process of buy-in works in four steps: from 1) exposure to active learning, to 2) persuasion that these activities are good, to 3) identification that the activities are good for them personally, to 4) commitment to this way of learning." Each stage is hypothesized to depend on appraisals made at previous stages, culminating in engagement in self-regulated learning. The model was adapted from a faculty pedagogy-adoption model (Aragón et al., 2016) and tested via serial mediation in this course.
requirements: Students must first be clearly exposed to and understand active-learning activities before persuasion, identification, and commitment can be measured
constraints: The authors state the model is not causally tested and the interpretive scope is limited by cross-sectional data from a single course
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students in required science courses
target_learning_goals: engagement in self-regulated learning
adoption of active-learning participation behaviors
examples: The model was tested in a 2000-level Human Anatomy and Physiology course of 363 enrollments using a 16-activity buy-in survey and serial mediation analysis
key_sources: Cavanagh A. J., Aragón O. R., Chen X., Couch B., Durham M., Bobrownicki A., Hanauer D. I., Graham M. J. (2016). Student Buy-In to Active Learning in a College Science Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education 15(4). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-07-0212

article_title: Student Buy-In to Active Learning in a College Science Course.
citation: Cavanagh A. J., Aragón O. R., Chen X., Couch B., Durham M., Bobrownicki A., Hanauer D. I., Graham M. J. (2016). Student Buy-In to Active Learning in a College Science Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education 15(4). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-07-0212
title: 16-item EPIC buy-in survey protocol for active-learning pedagogies
description: A survey instrument measuring student buy-in across a "discrete set of 16 empirically supported active-learning pedagogies detailed in the scientific teaching taxonomy." Exposure is measured as "I did this" / "I did not do this" / "I did this but did not understand it," and students who engaged in an activity answer yes/no items for persuasion, identification, and commitment; yes responses are summed (0–16) per EPIC category. Supplementary items gauge liking and obligation. Domains covered include active learning, assessment, and inclusivity.
requirements: Activities included must be clear and relevant to the specific course being surveyed
constraints: The instrument was administered once, near the end of the semester, in a single course section
target_learners: undergraduate students in active-learning science courses
target_learning_goals: measuring student buy-in to active learning
examples: Sample items include "I answered questions in class using a clicker or other polling method" and "I considered the contributions of diverse people and perspectives in the realm of scientific discovery"

article_title: Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics
citation: Rachel E. Scherr and David Hammer. (2007). Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics. Submitted to Cognition and Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/0711.0417
title: Epistemological framing as a locally coherent pattern of activated epistemological resources
description: The article develops epistemological framing from anthropology and linguistics: to frame an activity is to interpret it based on previous experience, bringing a structure of expectations about what could happen, what deserves attention, and what action is appropriate. In the resource-based account, a frame is "a locally coherent pattern of activations" of epistemological resources, linking individual cognition with group dynamics.
requirements: Analysis requires observational data on verbal, paraverbal, and nonverbal cues in the interaction, not only on what people say.
constraints: Frames are local and time-bound: their coherence may be particular to the moment or context, so a frame identification describes the episode rather than a stable trait.
target_learners: introductory university physics students working in collaborative tutorial groups
target_learning_goals: students' epistemological framing of learning activities — how they understand what knowledge, reasoning, and learning in physics entail
examples: Jasmin's singsong, arms-hugging reading from the worksheet versus her louder, gesturing comment that "This is like one of the questions" shows behavior matching the substance of speech.
key_sources: Rachel E. Scherr and David Hammer. (2007). Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics. Submitted to Cognition and Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/0712.0211

article_title: Reinventing College Physics for Biologists: Explicating an epistemological curriculum
citation: Edward F. Redish and David Hammer. (2009). Reinventing College Physics for Biologists: Explicating an epistemological curriculum. https://www.physics.umd.edu/perg/papers/redish/AAPT2009RedishHammer.pdf
title: Epistemologized curriculum: making implicit epistemological content explicit across all course components
description: The reform treats every course component — lecture, tutorials, labs, homework, exams, and course center — as carrying an implicit epistemological curriculum that must be made explicit and aligned. A shared vocabulary (shopping for ideas, sense making, seeking coherence, restricting the scope, choosing foothold ideas, playing the implications game) with icons was integrated across lectures and materials. The authors made "every effort to try to get all the parts of the class to work together and send the same epistemological message," modifying existing best-practices materials rather than replacing them.
requirements: All course components must send a consistent epistemological meta-message
Existing best-practices materials must be modified to avoid cognitive-conflict side effects that teach students to set intuition aside
constraints: Retains traditional structure in time and instructional personnel; the authors had to compromise substantially on extent and quality of homework feedback due to TA load
target_learners: college students in large introductory physics service courses
target_learning_goals: epistemological development
learning to think scientifically
building coherence and mechanism-based reasoning
examples: Lecturer created PowerPoint icons reinforcing epistemological framings; tutorials and ILDs included the same icons used in lecture
key_sources: Edward F. Redish and David Hammer. (2009). Reinventing College Physics for Biologists: Explicating an epistemological curriculum. https://www.physics.umd.edu/perg/papers/redish/AAPT2009RedishHammer.pdf

article_title: Using Warrants As a Window to Epistemic Framing
citation: Thomas J. Bing and Edward F. Redish. (2008). Using Warrants As a Window to Epistemic Framing. PERC 2008. https://www.compadre.org/PER/
title: Three epistemic framings of mathematics use in physics: Physical Mapping, Invoking Authority, and Calculation
description: The article names three epistemic framings of mathematics use in physics: Physical Mapping, Invoking Authority, and Calculation. Because "Math in physics can have many different natures: it can be a computational scheme, reflect a physical idea, conveniently encode a rule, and so forth," a student's current framing selects which subset of mathematical knowledge is active and what justifications count.
requirements: Identifying a student's framing requires access to their mathematical arguments, spoken or written, so that their warrants can be tracked.
constraints: The authors do not claim the three framings represent rigidly compartmentalized modes of thought; they have often observed mixings, like a student using a calculation scheme to back up a physical intuition.
target_learning_goals: epistemic framing of mathematics in physics problem solving
examples: S1's longer-path argument, S2's path-independence rule citation, and S1's call to solve each integral numerically.
key_sources: Thomas J. Bing and Edward F. Redish. (2008). Using Warrants As a Window to Epistemic Framing. PERC 2008. https://www.compadre.org/PER/

article_title: Using Warrants As a Window to Epistemic Framing
citation: Thomas J. Bing and Edward F. Redish. (2008). Using Warrants As a Window to Epistemic Framing. PERC 2008. https://www.compadre.org/PER/
title: Epistemic resources and framing as a cognitive model of in-the-moment knowledge use
description: The paper applies two cognitive modeling ideas to physics problem solving. Epistemic resources "activate and deactivate, leading a student to adopt a certain stance towards the physics knowledge at hand." Framing is the often subconscious answer to "What kind of activity is going on here?", selecting a subset of the person's knowledge for the situation.
requirements: Modeling in-the-moment reasoning requires fine-grained evidence such as video of students' speech and gesture during problem solving.
constraints: Epistemic stances are highly sensitive to context, and framing is often subconscious, so it must be inferred from indirect evidence such as warrants.
target_learning_goals: adopting productive epistemic stances toward physics knowledge
examples: A student may build a story explaining a result, treating knowledge as personally constructed, then turn to a textbook rule, treating knowledge as handed down from authority.
key_sources: Thomas J. Bing and Edward F. Redish. (2008). Using Warrants As a Window to Epistemic Framing. PERC 2008. https://www.compadre.org/PER/

article_title: On the formulation of Electrodynamics in a form independent of units
citation: C. Vrejoiu. (2008). On the formulation of Electrodynamics in a form independent of units. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/0812.0794
title: The epsilon-0, mu-0, c0 notation system for unit-independent electrodynamics
description: A notation set introduced from the alpha, lambda, gamma constants via epsilon-0-tilde = 1/alpha, mu-0-tilde = 1/lambda, c0 = 1/gamma, presented in Table 2 as "The ˜ε0, ˜µ0, c0-system". With it, Maxwell's equations take an SI-like form in which differences from SI are "reprezented by the presence of c0". The author states "The motivation for such notation is a pedagogical one" and traces it to earlier textbooks and lecture notes that used epsilon0 and mu0 from the beginning.
requirements: The constants are defined through the alpha, lambda, gamma system (equations 21) and specialize per unit system in Table 2
constraints: The notation differs from SI only through the presence of c0 in expressions such as the Lorentz force, energy current, potentials and field transformations
target_learners: students who know and use only SI
target_learning_goals: write and manipulate electrodynamics expressions in a form valid across unit systems while staying close to SI notation
examples: The article lists the SI-differing expressions: energy and momentum densities, Lorentz force F = qE + (1/c0) q v x B, field from potentials, gauge transformations, retardation solution, covariant 4-potential and field tensor
key_sources: C. Vrejoiu. (2008). On the formulation of Electrodynamics in a form independent of units. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/0812.0794

article_title: Analyzing Problem Solving Using Math in Physics: Epistemological Framing via Warrants
citation: Bing, T. J., & Redish, E. F. (2007). Analyzing Problem Solving Using Math in Physics: Epistemological Framing via Warrants. https://www.compadre.org/PER/
title: Epistemological framing: a student's judgment of what kind of knowledge applies in a situation
description: Epistemological framing is the usually subconscious process by which a student answers "What kind of activity is going on here?" and thereby narrows the set of mental options to a manageable subset. The authors define it as "a student's perception/judgment of the kind of knowledge that is appropriate to bring to bear in a particular situation". Framing is dynamic: people continually recheck and may alter it, bringing new resources into consideration while disregarding others. The paper builds it as a control-structure component of the Resource Framework for mathematics use in physics.
requirements: Analysis requires episodes where framing becomes explicit, such as disagreements between students, since framing is often unconscious
constraints: Framing is often unstated and even unconscious, so researchers access it indirectly through warrants
target_learning_goals: using mathematics effectively in physics problem solving
examples: Sarah's interview shift from quoting authority facts to constructing a conceptual story about electrical conduction after the interviewer's prompt
key_sources: Bing, T. J., & Redish, E. F. (2007). Analyzing Problem Solving Using Math in Physics: Epistemological Framing via Warrants. https://www.compadre.org/PER/

article_title: Examining the Impact of Student Expectations on Undergraduate Biology Education Reform
citation: Hall, K. L., Watkins, J. E., Coffey, J. E., Cooke, T. J., & Redish, E. F. (2011). Examining the Impact of Student Expectations on Undergraduate Biology Education Reform. AERA 2011. http://umdberg.pbworks.com/w/page/8039417/FrontPage
title: Epistemological expectations: students' beliefs about the nature of knowledge and what they should do to learn in a course
description: The article adopts the construct of expectations from the student epistemology literature, defining them as "a broad grouping of ideas that students might have about biology and biology learning that reflects on their in-class practice and activities." The analysis focuses on epistemological expectations: what students believe is the nature of the knowledge they are learning and what they should be doing to learn in a particular course. The framework is discipline-specific and context-driven, and the authors use it to interpret how students participate in and make sense of reformed course activities.
requirements: Analysis requires data sources in which expectations become salient, such as interviews where students discuss the effectiveness of class activities and their exam and homework strategies
constraints: The authors restrict their analysis to epistemological expectations rather than attitudes or epistemologies generally, and note the construct is discipline specific and context driven
target_learning_goals: understanding how students' views of knowledge shape their engagement with instruction
examples: Two expectations identified from iterative coding of 25 interviews were elaborated: knowledge as facts from authority, and math and physics as unnecessary for biology
key_sources: Hall, K. L., Watkins, J. E., Coffey, J. E., Cooke, T. J., & Redish, E. F. (2011). Examining the Impact of Student Expectations on Undergraduate Biology Education Reform. AERA 2011. http://umdberg.pbworks.com/w/page/8039417/FrontPage

article_title: Do Prescribed Prompts Prime Sensemaking During Group Problem Solving?
citation: Martinuk, M. and Ives, J. (2010). Do Prescribed Prompts Prime Sensemaking During Group Problem Solving? Physics Education Research conference proceedings style manuscript, University of British Columbia.
title: Epistemological framing coding scheme splitting Discussion into Procedural and Conceptual frames, with sensemaking operationalized as Conceptual Discussion
description: The article uses epistemological framing, "a person’s implicit expectations about knowledge and learning in their current activity and context," shared by members of a collaborative group. It modifies Scherr and Hammer's scheme in two ways: coding from audio alone matched video-plus-audio coding more than 80% of the time, and the Discussion frame was split into Procedural Discussion ("figuring out what to do") and Conceptual Discussion ("figuring out what is happening" in the physics). Sensemaking is operationalized as engaging in Conceptual Discussion.
requirements: Coders must reach consensus on Conceptual Discussion judgments; the authors achieved greater than 80% inter-rater reliability before discussion and 100% agreement after discussion.
constraints: Gradual transitions between the two Discussion frames caused coding disagreement and have not yet been incorporated into the coding scheme.
target_learners: introductory algebra-based physics students who did not take senior high school physics
target_learning_goals: expert-like problem solving
sensemaking of physics situations
examples: Six episodes of group problem solving were transcribed and coded frame-by-frame, with the time students reached each worksheet prompt also recorded.
key_sources: Martinuk, M. and Ives, J. (2010). Do Prescribed Prompts Prime Sensemaking During Group Problem Solving? Physics Education Research conference proceedings style manuscript, University of British Columbia. https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.5400

article_title: The role of context and culture in teaching physics: The implication of disciplinary differences
citation: Redish, E. F. (2012). The role of context and culture in teaching physics: The implication of disciplinary differences. Keynote address, World Conference on Physics Education 2012, Istanbul. https://www.physics.umd.edu
title: Epistemological framing: students' unconscious answer to what kind of knowledge is being learned and how to learn it controls their classroom behavior
description: Adapting Goffman's anthropological concept of framing, the article defines epistemological framing as "the process that generates each individual's answer to the questions: What is the nature of the knowledge we are learning in this class and what do I have to do to learn it?" Framing operates largely unconsciously, drawing on long-term memory to set expectations and control which knowledge and behaviors are activated. The article links it to neuroscience: pre-frontal cortex signals adjust attention and activate knowledge. Framing can have affective, social, and epistemological components, and mismatches between instructor and student framing can cause students to ignore intended messages.
requirements: Instructors must consider what socio-cultural knowledge the student brings, since "it's a student's perception of the socio-cultural environment that affects that student's behavior"
constraints: Framing is often unconscious, so students may not be aware of the expectations controlling their behavior
target_learning_goals: interpreting student responses to instruction in terms of context-dependent expectations
examples: The article interprets the ticker-tape recitation and the ATP bond quiz through epistemological framing
key_sources: Redish, E. F. (2012). The role of context and culture in teaching physics: The implication of disciplinary differences. Keynote address, World Conference on Physics Education 2012, Istanbul. https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.4840

article_title: Learning Each Others' Ropes: Negotiating interdisciplinary authenticity
citation: Edward F. Redish and Todd J. Cooke. (2012). Learning Each Other's Ropes: Negotiating interdisciplinary authenticity. To be published in CBE-LSE. http://umdberg.pbworks.com/w/page/8039417/FrontPage
title: The epistemologized algebra-based physics course: a reform shifting student epistemologies from equations and factoids to coherent, principle-based reasoning.
description: Between 2000 and 2005, the physicist and UMd-PERG colleagues reformed the algebra-based physics class to make it more appropriate for life-science students, a project that "epistemologized best-practices research-based instructional methods". The reform "emphasized shifting student epistemologies", moving learners "from pieces to coherence, from equations to concepts, from externally-transferred knowledge to internally-generated reasoning". The article reports the course "showed strong gains on both standardized conceptual and attitudinal measures" but did not significantly modify content for life-science needs.
requirements: Research-based instructional methods as a starting point
Emphasis on shifting student epistemologies toward coherence and internally-generated reasoning
constraints: The course did not significantly modify content to accommodate the needs of life science students, in part because the course served other populations as well
target_learners: undergraduate life-science students and pre-meds in algebra-based introductory physics
target_learning_goals: view physics knowledge as coherent and principle-based rather than as independent factoids and equations to memorize
examples: The reformed course showed strong gains on both standardized conceptual and attitudinal measures (Redish & Hammer, 2009)
key_sources: Edward F. Redish and Todd J. Cooke. (2012). Learning Each Other's Ropes: Negotiating interdisciplinary authenticity. To be published in CBE-LSE. http://umdberg.pbworks.com/w/page/8039417/FrontPage

article_title: Beyond deficit-based models of learners' cognition: Interpreting engineering students' difficulties with sense-making in terms of fine-grained epistemological and conceptual dynamics
citation: Gupta, A., & Elby, A. (2011). Beyond deficit-based models of learners' cognition: Interpreting engineering students' difficulties with sense-making in terms of fine-grained epistemological and conceptual dynamics. Submitted to Journal of Engineering Education.
title: Epistemological variability: epistemologies as context-dependent local coherences of epistemological resources rather than globally robust beliefs
description: The article adopts the Redish–Hammer cognitive theory in which epistemological variability is accounted for by "the context-dependent activation of locally coherent networks of epistemological 'resources' (pieces of knowledge about knowledge)." Different contextual cues and mental states foreground different aspects of a student's epistemology, so what looks like a robust belief can be a locally stable stance. The authors use this framework to interpret Jim's shifting stance during the interview.
requirements: Analysis must attend to contextual cues and the student's conceptual and emotional state, not only to stated beliefs
constraints: The authors state this work illustrates, but cannot prove as a general rule, the explanatory power of viewing epistemologies as context-dependent local coherences
target_learning_goals: mathematical sense-making in physics problem solving
examples: Jim's stance shifted when the interviewer prompted him about the sign of g in the hydrostatic pressure equation
key_sources: Gupta, A., & Elby, A. (2011). article_title: Oersted Lecture 2013: How should we think about how our students think?
citation: Edward F. Redish. (2013). Oersted Lecture 2013: How should we think about how our students think? http://www.physics.umd.edu/perg/abp/TPProbs/Problems/E/E67.htm
title: Epistemological framing: students' in-the-moment perception of the nature of the knowledge a task calls for
description: Epistemological framing is the control structure by which a student, facing a knowledge-constructing task, decides "what is going on" and restricts the search space of long-term memory — what knowledge is relevant and how to approach the task. The author adapts framing from Goffman's anthropology and sociolinguistics, defining it as "the process of choosing different ways and tools of knowing (epistemological resources) for dealing with learning situations." It restricts the conceptual, associational, and epistemological resources students access in a given context, and the related term epistemological stance names the resulting functional state. Classroom video data show mis-framings leading students to fail to access knowledge they actually have.
requirements: Videotaped observation of students working in groups or interviews to see framing in action
Attention to the student's perception of the socio-cultural environment, not just the environment itself
constraints: Framing decisions are not necessarily conscious
The same framing can be appropriate in some situations and lead to trouble in others
target_learners: Physics students from introductory college to graduate school
target_learning_goals: Accessing relevant knowledge during problem solving
Developing productive epistemological stances toward learning physics
examples: The author's instructions in the pass-counting demonstration encouraged a concentration framing that suppressed noticing other events

article_title: The Use of Epistemic Distancing to Create a Safe Space to Sensemake in Introductory Physics Tutorials
citation: Luke D. Conlin. (2012). The use of epistemic distancing to create a safe space to sensemake in introductory physics tutorials. http://spu.edu/depts/physics/tcp/tadevelopment.asp
title: Epistemic distancing: discourse moves that soften a speaker's stance to protect affect during idea sharing
description: The article defines epistemic distancing as "Any discourse move by which speakers soften their stance, including hedging, joking, and deferring." It is "epistemic" because it concerns the speaker's commitment to the truth of what they say, and "distancing" because it "creates distance between the speaker and what they are saying," which "protects the speaker's affect in the event that the idea gets evaluated negatively, thereby reducing ego threat." The construct covers hedging phrases like "I think," quoting others, deferring, phrasing claims as questions, rising intonation, and body positioning.
requirements: A group discussion context in which students risk having their ideas evaluated negatively by peers or instructors
constraints: The article notes that "more epistemic distancing is necessarily better" is not the case: students who distance themselves too much "can come across as so dismissive of the activity that they discourage further contributions"
target_learners: introductory physics students in active-engagement tutorials
target_learning_goals: collaborative sensemaking about physical mechanisms
contributing and evaluating ideas in group discussion
examples: Daria hedging an idea with "Maybe it's just getting started up or something"; Chrissie's laughter marking a lack of seriousness; Chrissie deferring to the worksheet by reading the next question
key_sources: Luke D. Conlin. (2012). The use of epistemic distancing to create a safe space to sensemake in introductory physics tutorials. http://spu.edu/depts/physics/tcp/tadevelopment.asp

article_title: Play or science?: a study of learning and framing in crowdscience games
citation: Lieberoth, A., Pedersen, M. K., & Sherson, J. F. (2015). Play or Science? A Study of Learning and Framing in Crowdscience. Aarhus University, Centre for Community Driven Research (CODER). https://scienceathome.org/games/quantum-dreams/
title: Epistemic frame oscillation in crowdscience games
description: The article adapts Goffmanian frame analysis to crowdscience play: "Frames can be understood as the shifting lenses through which we interpret social reality beyond the immediate physical givens." In Quantum Dreams, the gamelike GUI keyed a swing to a gaming frame from an initial education/science frame, and players' descriptions were coded as game, science, or conceptual. The authors conclude the special status of crowdscience games "affords some cognitive freedom: An ecology of thinking-layers to oscillate within."
requirements: Interpretive frames must be keyed by both the game interface and the surrounding educational or scientific situation for oscillation to occur
constraints: The supporting study examined one Danish vocational class playing an early game version, with a rough heuristic categorization of descriptions and no a priori analysis criteria
target_learners: Danish vocational (HTX) students aged 14-22 who are heavy gamers with high physics interest
target_learning_goals: Describing game interface elements in physics terms
Interpreting quantum atom-transport gameplay
examples: After a physics talk introduced the game at a vocational school, the gamelike GUI keyed a swing to gaming from which some students were not able to shift back

article_title: Epistemic Impact on Group Problem Solving for Different Science Majors
citation: Andrew J. Mason, Charles A. Bertram. (2014). Epistemic Impact on Group Problem Solving for Different Science Majors. US-China Education Review B. https://www.davidpublisher.org
title: Epistemic games framework (Tuminaro & Redish) for categorizing students' problem-solving approaches
description: The article applies the epistemic games framework of Tuminaro and Redish (2007), in which students' problem-solving behavior is analyzed as the invocation of named games such as Recursive Plug and Chug, Mapping Mathematics to Meaning, Pictorial Analysis, and Transliteration to Maths. The authors identified games from transcribed audiovisual lab-group data corroborated with written reflection rubrics, noting a student "realized one equation for torque does not address the unknown quantity of angular acceleration, and opted for another equation that does." The framework serves as the coding scheme linking group epistemic orientation to game choice.
requirements: Transcribed observational data of group problem solving plus corroborating reflection rubrics to identify which epistemic games students invoke
constraints: The article codes games from a single late-semester lesson on rotational dynamics at one institution
target_learners: undergraduate life science, health science, chemistry, and computer science majors in introductory physics
target_learning_goals: physics problem-solving skills
epistemic views toward physics
examples: A framework-oriented student's rubric on a rotational dynamics lab problem showed a Recursive Plug and Chug game and hints of a Mapping Mathematics to Meaning game.

article_title: Analysing the Competency of Mathematical Modelling in Physics
citation: Edward F. Redish. (2015). Analysing the Competency of Mathematical Modelling in Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0608268
title: Epistemological resources, framing, and stances as three lenses on how students justify physics knowledge
description: The article develops three ways to talk about how students use knowledge: epistemological resources (generalized "How do we know?" warrants such as physical intuition, trust in calculation, trusted authority, physical mapping to math, fundamental laws, and toy models), epistemological framing (the process of deciding which resources are relevant, not necessarily conscious), and epistemological stances (coherent sets of resources often activated together as a go-to approach). A meta-resource, coherence, holds that multiple ways of knowing should yield the same result.
requirements: Instructional design should account for students' epistemological framing, since students may not call on resources they are competent with
constraints: The article cautions these are NOT intended to describe distinct mental structures, only different aspects of activating a subset of knowledge in a situation
target_learners: biology students in interdisciplinary physics courses
target_learning_goals: epistemological sophistication in mathematical modeling
choosing appropriate warrants in physics problem solving
examples: Three students discussing a path-independence homework problem used different warrants - physical intuition, numerical calculation, and a remembered theorem - and reached agreement after about 15 minutes
key_sources: Edward F. Redish. (2015). Analysing the Competency of Mathematical Modelling in Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.02966

article_title: Examining and contrasting the cognitive activities engaged in undergraduate research experiences and lab courses
citation: N.G. Holmes and Carl E. Wieman. (2016). Examining and contrasting the cognitive activities engaged in undergraduate research experiences and lab courses. https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.01422
title: Experimental Physics Cognitive Task Analysis (EPCTA) framework
description: The EPCTA is a framework of eight cognitive task elements used by physicists to carry out an experiment from conception to completion, defined by Wieman as the "mental tasks or types of thinking ('cognitive task analysis') associated with a physicist doing tabletop experimental research". The elements span establishing research goals, defining criteria for suitable evidence, determining feasibility, experimental design, construction and testing of apparatus/code, analyzing data, evaluating results, and presenting the work. This article uses the EPCTA as the coding lens for characterizing students' cognitive processes in UREs and coursework, noting the process is highly iterative and cyclic rather than linear.
requirements: Each task element contains sub-tasks, and moving through the EPCTA often occurs in a highly iterative and cyclic process
constraints: Developed in the context of experimental physics, though the authors note many elements are fundamental skills benefiting students in a variety of contexts
target_learning_goals: scientific experimentation skills and practices
understanding the process of experimental research
examples: The article coded focus group discussions of 32 URE students by EPCTA element and context (research, lecture, structured lab, design lab), summarized in Fig. 3 and Table II
key_sources: N.G. Holmes and Carl E. Wieman. (2016). Examining and contrasting the cognitive activities engaged in undergraduate research experiences and lab courses. https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.01422

article_title: Potential relationship of epistemic games to group dynamics and learning orientations towards physics problem solving
citation: Andrew J. Mason and Charles A. Bertram. (2015). Potential Relationship of Epistemic Games to Group Dynamics and Learning Orientations towards Physics Problem Solving. University of Central Arkansas. https://www.compadre.org/PER/
title: Epistemic games as structures of knowledge and strategy in physics problem solving
description: The article adopts Tuminaro and Redish's definition of "epistemic games" as "structures of knowledge and strategy as employed into physics problem solving". The games are named and placed in approximate order of most to least intellectually complex: Mapping Meaning to Mathematics, Mapping Mathematics to Meaning, Physical Mechanism, Pictorial Analysis, Recursive Plug and Chug, and Transliteration to Mathematics. The article uses this framework to quantify students' game choices from audiovisual recordings.
requirements: Audiovisual recordings of group problem solving, normalized by total recording time, to estimate game frequencies
constraints: The article notes some games are more intellectually complex than others and that less deep games contain a risk of superficial learning
target_learning_goals: physics problem solving strategies
examples: Students recorded in brief 1-2 minute samplings across three semesters, with games per minute computed per group
key_sources: Andrew J. Mason and Charles A. Bertram. (2015). Potential Relationship of Epistemic Games to Group Dynamics and Learning Orientations towards Physics Problem Solving. University of Central Arkansas. https://www.compadre.org/PER/

article_title: Toolboxes and handing students a hammer: The effects of cueing and instruction on getting students to think critically
citation: N.G. Holmes, Dhaneesh Kumar and D.A. Bonn. (2017). Toolboxes and handing students a hammer: The effects of cueing and instruction on getting students to think critically. https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.07017
title: Epistemological frames and task orientation as the explanatory lens for cueing effects on lab behavior
description: The article interprets students' experimentation behaviors through epistemological frames, defined as "the student’s perception or judgment of the kind of knowledge that is appropriate to bring to bear in a particular situation", and task orientation, "interpreting task demands and then direct[ing] further learning activities accordingly". Prior SQILabs instruction fosters sensemaking frames, while subtle procedural cues can elicit rote-procedure frames, shifting which tools students apply. The framework distinguishes representational tools, which frame analysis as a concluding act, from inferential tools, which frame analysis as a step toward making sense of data.
requirements: Inference of frames requires tasks with observable decision points, such as common measurement mistakes and systematic effects that students must choose how to resolve
constraints: The study examines cohort-level common resources rather than individual frames; the authors note it is less clear whether behavioral cues can also trigger sensemaking frames over procedural ones
target_learners: introductory physics lab students at a large research-intensive university
