article_title: Blending physical knowledge with mathematical form in physics problem solving
citation: Mark Eichenlaub, Edward F. Redish. (2018). Blending physical knowledge with mathematical form in physics problem solving. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.01639
title: Epistemic games framework for analyzing student problem-solving moves and motivations
description: An epistemic game is a script that structures the types of resources students call on and the order in which they use them during problem solving. The framework, drawing on Tuminaro and Redish's version, models problem-solving as moves (mathematical, conversational, or physical) that gradually fill out an epistemological form—a template for what the solution should look like. The authors use this framework to analyze how students blend physical intuition with mathematical formalism during scaffolded problem-solving interviews. Different games have different rules about what evidence is salient, what moves are allowed, and what it means to be done.
requirements: The framework requires identifying which epistemic game a student is playing to understand the resources they call on and the order of use
constraints: The framework is analytical, not prescriptive—it is used as a lens for researchers rather than steps for students to follow
target_learning_goals: physics problem solving
mathematical sensemaking in physics
examples: The authors analyzed student interviews using games such as sanity check, dimensional analysis, and significant features

article_title: Student Epistemological Framing on Paper-Based Assessments
citation: Kelli Shar, Rosemary S. Russ, James T. Laverty. (2021). Student Epistemological Framing on Paper-Based Assessments. https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.07442
title: Epistemological framing and resources model applied to assessment contexts
description: This framework treats a student's in-the-moment epistemology as an epistemological framing—the tacit stance a student takes toward a learning activity—understood as a local coherence of finer-grained epistemological resources assembled anew in each context. The authors apply it to assessment, hypothesizing that "understanding the speciﬁc resources that make up the framings will give us more insight into how and why students engage in learning in particular ways than merely identifying their epis- temological framings as a whole." Framings are contextual and dynamic rather than stable across time and place, and resources span knowledge type, source, epistemic activity, and epistemic form.
requirements: Analysis requires observable behaviors or utterances from which frames and resources can be inferred, such as video-recorded think-aloud problem solving
constraints: The framework was applied to summative, constructed-response, paper-based physics assessment items with introductory students; the authors note epistemology in undergraduate physics assessment had not previously been directly examined
target_learners: undergraduate introductory calculus-based physics students, predominantly engineering majors
target_learning_goals: students' epistemological engagement with physics assessment problems
understanding what it means to know and do physics in assessment contexts
examples: The authors coded 67 problem-solving attempts for frames by behavior and a 20-instance subset for resources by full sentence, using categories from Hammer and Elby plus emergent codes such as Equation Sheet as a Knowledge Source

citation: Jessica R. Hoehn, Julian D. Gifford, and Noah D. Finkelstein. (2020). Epistemic stances toward group work in learning physics: Interactions between epistemology and social dynamics in a collaborative problem solving context. https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.02425
title: Epistemic stances toward group work: views about how group work functions to generate and apply knowledge, at the intersection of epistemology and group work
description: The article defines epistemic stances toward group work as "views about how group work functions to generate and apply knowledge, existing at the intersection of these two domains" of epistemology and group work (Fig. 1). The construct is finer-grained than epistemological framing: it isolates the epistemic aspect of group work expectations from social norms, accountability, and general views about learning physics. The authors use it as an analytic lens to investigate how epistemology and social dynamics interact in collaborative problem solving, and to explain why a cohesive group frame can still produce inequitable positioning of individual members.

article_title: Investigating Unprompted and Prompted Diagrams Generated by Physics MajorsDuring Problem Solving
citation: Vignal, M., & Wilcox, B. R. (2021). Investigating Unprompted and Prompted Diagrams Generated by Physics Majors During Problem Solving. arXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.07765
title: Epistemic frames and the distributed cognition framework for interpreting student diagrams
description: The article frames unprompted and prompted diagramming as occurring in different epistemic frames — the perspective a learner has for an educational setting or task — such that unprompted diagrams are generated for the student's own problem solving while prompted diagrams are generated for someone else. It pairs this with the distributed cognition framework, which "holds that people will externalize (e.g., generate a diagram) for two main reasons: to reduce their cognitive load or to communicate information." Together these frameworks let the authors interpret diagram features as signposts of cognitive processes rather than deficits, since externalizations are expected to differ when done for these two reasons.
requirements: Interview or task contexts must suppress cues that diagrams are expected or assessed so that unprompted diagrams reflect the student's own problem-solving goals
constraints: The article notes studies gathering diagrams from homework and exams must be interpreted in the context of those assignments, where diagrams are generally encouraged and often explicitly assessed
target_learning_goals: problem solving
use of diagrammatic representations in physics
examples: Interview participants were told the goal was to get the correct answer but were not asked to show work or draw diagrams, placing them in a problem-solving epistemic frame; the final six items asked them to carefully generate and label a diagram with no actual problem to solve, an explicitly communicative epistemic frame

citation: Jamal Mimouni. (2022). On making physics relevant to society in general and to scientists in particular: Closing the epistemic gap. Proceedings of the African Conference on Fundamental and Applied Physics (ACP2021). https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.06728
title: The epistemic gap between physics teaching and the physicist's understanding
description: The article's organizing concept is an 'epistemic gap' between how physics is taught and what genuine understanding of physics entails. The abstract names 'the need to close the epistemic gap between physics teaching and the physicist's understanding.' The gap arises because teaching emphasizes problem-solving tricks and utilitarian applications while the discipline's essence lies in its conceptual, cognitive dimension, which the author says can fire up imagination and kindle genuine vocations. Closing the gap means re-centering teaching on concepts, explanation, and the simplicity and coherence of fundamental laws.
requirements: Teaching must engage the conceptual part of physics, which the author identifies as the discipline's core
constraints: The author frames the argument for physics education in his African/Algerian context, noting conceptual-physics books are not much known or used in African countries
target_learning_goals: genuine conceptual understanding of physics
vocation and motivation in physics
examples: The author cites conceptual physics books and Feynman's lectures as resources appealing to the conceptual part of physics

article_title: How well-intentioned white male physicists maintain ignorance of inequity and justify inaction
citation: Melissa Dancy & Apriel K. Hodari. (2022). How well-intentioned white male physicists maintain ignorance of inequity and justify inaction.
title: Epistemology of ignorance: ignorance of racism and sexism among the privileged is actively produced and serves to maintain white and male supremacy.
description: The article adopts the epistemology of ignorance (Sullivan & Tuana, 2007) as its theoretical framing. It posits that ignorance is not a mere gap in knowledge but, in the authors' words, "ignorance serves the interests of those in privileged positions (i.e. white men) and is therefore cultivated and maintained by systems of power". The framework guides the analysis by asking what these men do not know, how their not knowing supports dominance, and by what mechanisms they maintain ignorance despite abundant nearby information.
requirements: Analysis must use a critical discourse lens, since the mechanisms operate without the awareness or intent of the speakers.
constraints: The article applies the framing specifically to race and gender privilege among progressive white men in US physics departments.
target_learners: white male physics faculty and graduate students
target_learning_goals: recognizing racism and sexism in one's own environment
understanding one's own complicity in maintaining inequity
examples: The authors used the framing to ask how otherwise highly intelligent and successful physicists maintain high levels of ignorance of sexism, racism and their own privilege.

citation: Ian Descamps, Sophia Jeon, N. G. Holmes, Rachel E. Scherr, and David Hammer. (2024). Dynamics of Productive Confirmation Framing in an Introductory Lab. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.14526

constraints: Framing is understood to conceptualize aspects of highly complex dynamics involving multiple scales of time and system
